clue.text: Reading Dante in new form of a royal idyll

indicators.note: the letters of the three preceding words are recast into a new shape, so this phrase signals rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone reads Dante and recasts him as a poem about kings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in new form' rearranges READINGDANTEIN into the title of one of Tennyson's Idylls of the King, the Arthurian poems about the court of King Arthur.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's Idylls of the King includes a poem with this title about a knight of the Round Table and his wife.

clue.text: Crikey! A short week and we get the bird

parts.note: both are mild exclamations of surprise
WK is the usual abbreviation of week

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a short working week brings a sighting of some bird.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a large hawk once much used in falconry.

clue.text: CO's au pair is uncommonly like a harpy

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests the letters of the fodder appear in an unusual order

parts.note: CO's taken as written, the apostrophe ignored, giving the letters C, O and S

explanation.surface: A commanding officer's nanny proves strikingly grasping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' shuffles COSAUPAIR. A harpy in Greek myth is a snatching monster, so 'like a harpy' means grasping and greedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Harpies are mythical snatchers, so being like one means being greedy and grasping.

clue.text: What's empty in an Englishman's head ?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, taken here from Englishman's

explanation.surface: A jibe asking what lies inside an Englishman's skull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' takes the first letter E of 'Englishman's'; IN and AN are the clue's own words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something empty of sense or content is silly and vacuous.

clue.text: Diplomacy here, abroad needs an adept in battle

parts.note: tact is diplomacy in dealing with others
ici is French for here, abroad pointing to a foreign language
needs is a link and an gives the letters as written

explanation.surface: Diplomacy overseas calls for someone skilled at warfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' says 'here' is to be turned into French.
explanation.definitionFit: A tactician is someone skilled in the deployment of forces in battle.

clue.text: See 1
A drunkard consumes many of course

indicators.note: the drunkard swallowing something means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, standing for many

explanation.surface: Naturally, a drinker puts away plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally', but 'course' is the definition: ASCOT is a racecourse in Berkshire, England, home of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a famous English racecourse.

clue.text: Golfing conservative unbeatable in this suburb ?

definitions.text: Golfing conservative unbeatable in this suburb ?

parts.words: Golfing conservative unbeatable in this suburb ?
parts.note: a golfer who cannot lose the match is 'dormy', and a Conservative is a Tory: say the two together and you have the kind of suburb where commuters sleep

explanation.surface: A Conservative golfer who cannot be beaten lives in a commuter suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf a player is 'dormy' when ahead by as many holes as remain, so cannot lose. A 'dormy Tory' sounds like the commuter suburb where people only sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A suburb whose residents work elsewhere and only sleep there is called this kind of suburb.

clue.text: "That last infirmity of —— mind" (Milton)

parts.note: a line from Milton's Lycidas about fame, with the adjective before 'mind' left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.walkthrough: Milton's Lycidas calls fame 'That last infirmity of noble mind'; the word missing from the quotation is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Milton's line describes a lofty, high-minded character.

clue.text: Power-house

parts.note: read not as a generating station but as a house, in the sense of a family line, that holds power

explanation.walkthrough: A 'power-house' is usually a generating station; here it is a ruling family, a house that holds power.
explanation.definitionFit: A succession of rulers from one family is a ruling house.

clue.text: Brown is sanctimonious in the main

indicators.note: in places the sanctimonious word inside the sea

parts.note: the main is a poetic name for the open sea
pi is short for pious, meaning sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A dark-skinned figure is self-righteous while at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Sepia is a reddish-brown colour, from cuttlefish ink.

clue.text: Early whodunit victim

parts.note: the nursery rhyme asking 'Who killed ...?' reads as the earliest murder mystery, and its bird is the victim

explanation.surface: Who died first in a detective story?
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Who killed ...?' asks who shot the bird with a bow and arrow, so its victim is the first murder in a whodunit.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird killed by the sparrow in the old nursery rhyme is the victim of an early murder mystery.

clue.text: Subtle Jonsonian, an apprentice pharmacist ?

parts.note: an gives A, the indefinite article
L for learner, as on the plates of a learner driver, stands for an apprentice
in Britain a chemist is a pharmacist

explanation.surface: A clever character from Ben Jonson is a trainee dispenser of medicines.
explanation.walkthrough: Subtle is the title character of Ben Jonson's comedy of 1610, a con man posing as a maker of gold.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jonson's play the swindler called Subtle poses as a gold-maker, the title role.

clue.text: Thoughts may be said to be without point

annotationWithheld.why: Thoughts may be said to be without point (5): IDEAS; 'Thoughts' defines it, but no reading found for 'may be said to be without point'.
annotationWithheld.clue: Thoughts may be said to be without point

clue.text: Up North nothing is heard of this scourge

indicators.note: is heard means the word is taken as spoken, a matching sound with different spelling

parts.note: nowt is northern English dialect for nothing

explanation.surface: In the north of England, nothing is said about this whip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up North' points to northern English dialect, where 'nowt' means nothing; the scourge, a Russian whip, is said the same with its K silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A knout was a Russian whip used to flog criminals.

clue.text: Unintelligent chump, but hardly cracked ?

definitions.meaning: a skull so thick that it would be hard to crack

explanation.surface: A dunce, but at least not mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracked' looks like 'crazy'; read literally it is a skull that would not break easily.
explanation.definitionFit: A dim fool has a dense skull, and a dense skull is not easily broken.

clue.text: Dishonesty? I'm for getting by without it

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
pro means in favour of, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so by goes around it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they are in favour of dishonesty when managing without it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking', but here it has its old sense 'outside', so one piece wraps the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Probity is honesty, so its opposite is dishonesty.

clue.text: A tidy one, we read, the Elephant's Child

definitions.meaning: in Kipling's Just So Stories the hero is described as a tidy specimen of thick-skinned beast
the young elephant, hero of Kipling's tale, is a thick-skinned mammal

explanation.walkthrough: In Kipling's 'The Elephant's Child', from the Just So Stories, the young elephant is called 'a Tidy Pachyderm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephants are classed as thick-skinned mammals, and Kipling's story calls the young hero a tidy one.

clue.text: Such things are not to be made any longer

definitions.text: Such things are not to be made any longer

parts.words: Such things are not to be made any longer
parts.note: looks like a product line being discontinued, but means things that cannot be stretched

explanation.surface: A manufacturer announces that a product line has been discontinued.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to be made any longer' sounds like 'discontinued' but means they cannot be stretched to greater length.
explanation.definitionFit: Material that cannot be stretched lacks springiness or give.

clue.text: Like Handel's work describing Isaiah's prophecies

definitions.meaning: the Book of Isaiah foretells a coming saviour

explanation.surface: Handel's oratorio sets the prophet's words about a saviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to a promised saviour, as in Handel's oratorio and the prophecies of Isaiah.

clue.text: Model of keenness on board

definitions.meaning: the phrase 'keen as' a hot condiment
the colonel of that name is a character on the Cluedo board game

explanation.surface: A model employee is enthusiastic once taken on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen as mustard' is a British idiom for very eager; Colonel Mustard is a suspect in the board game Cluedo (Clue in America).
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'keen as' this condiment makes it a byword for eagerness, and a Cluedo suspect bears the name.

clue.text: Crop figure may be of interest

definitions.meaning: the percentage return paid on an investment

explanation.surface: A farmer's harvest figure might attract attention.
explanation.definitionFit: A harvest's output and an investment's percentage return are both called this.

clue.text: Merit of French verse perhaps

parts.note: de is French for of

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of verse may be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A judge assesses the worth of some French poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges VERSE into SERVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To merit something is to be worthy of it.

clue.text: A 2 swimmer has a "suitable" skin

definitions.meaning: a greedy predator of the sea, 2 pointing to the down clue meaning grasping
sharkskin is a smooth fabric used for suits

explanation.walkthrough: '2' refers to the answer to 2 Down, meaning grasping. 'suitable' in quotes means fit for a suit: sharkskin is a cloth used for suits.
explanation.definitionFit: A greedy sea predator, and its name is given to a fabric used for suits.

clue.text: Fish may be obtuse

definitions.meaning: to fish with a rod and line
a geometric figure greater than ninety degrees

explanation.surface: A fish can be dim.
explanation.definitionFit: To fish with a line, and a figure in geometry that can exceed ninety degrees.

clue.text: Says a bone can be a source of sauce

indicators.note: can be says the letters may be made into another word

explanation.surface: Someone claims a bone can supply sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' rearranges SAYSABONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Fermented soy, made from these legumes, gives soy sauce.

clue.text: Turf out of the South hospital room

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south
a ward is a room for patients in a hospital

explanation.surface: Someone is thrown out of a southern hospital room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turf out' looks like 'evict', but 'Turf' alone is the definition and 'out of' joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sward is an expanse of grass, turf.

clue.text: Shakespeare's porcine ghost ?

parts.note: the philosopher once claimed as the true author of the plays, a ghost writer whose name is also a cured pig meat

explanation.surface: A pig haunts the playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Some held that Francis Bacon wrote Shakespeare's plays, making him the ghost writer; bacon is also pig meat, hence 'porcine'.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon, the Elizabethan philosopher, was claimed by some as the true author of the plays, and the word means cured pork.

clue.text: Collect material for concrete

definitions.meaning: to gather together into a whole
the gravel or crushed stone mixed into cement

explanation.surface: Gather the ingredients for a concrete mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather into a mass, and the stone or gravel mixed with cement.

clue.text: Provide such a pillar for lepidopterists ?

definitions.meaning: to supply food or what is needed
put before 'pillar' it makes the larva of a butterfly or moth, studied by lepidopterists

explanation.surface: Supply a column for butterfly collectors.
explanation.walkthrough: Lepidopterists study butterflies and moths; the answer placed before 'pillar' makes their larva.
explanation.definitionFit: To supply food or what is needed, and the first half of a butterfly larva's name.

clue.text: Author Charles has divine exterior but is greatly feared

indicators.note: the divine is on the outside, so the author sits within it

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, stands for a divine or clergyman
Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth

explanation.surface: A writer with a clerical air is very much feared.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade (1814-84) wrote The Cloister and the Hearth; DD (Doctor of Divinity) is the standard crossword divine. 'has ... exterior' puts the divine outside the author.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dreaded is regarded with great fear.

clue.text: Cyclopian spectacle ?

parts.note: a Cyclops has one eye, so his spectacles would be a single lens

explanation.surface: A sight fit for a giant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spectacle' looks like a sight, but it is eyewear for one eye, as the one-eyed Cyclops would need.
explanation.definitionFit: A single eyeglass suits a one-eyed giant.
